assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics changed how economists treat institutions. Constitutions, electoral rules, accountability and state capacity are now endogenous objects of analysis rather than a fixed backdrop. The work joined formal theory to comparative empirical evidence and shaped later work on growth, development and fiscal policy. It also links closely to economic history, since state capacity and institutional persistence are long-run questions.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the central pair for the constitutional and electoral-rules programme. Besley is a close third, through the accountability and state-capacity work, including joint work with Persson. Other contributors (for example Acemoglu, Robinson and Alesina) fall outside the credited names, or the prize has already recognised them for adjacent institutional work. That makes the boundaries of the discovery a matter of judgment.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The core contributions date from the 1990s and 2000s and have had decades of replication, extension and use. There is no timing risk.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize for institutions and prosperity may reduce the committee's appetite for a closely related area.
The empirical identification of constitutional effects is contested.
The choice of three names from a broader field is partly arbitrary.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities is the workhorse of modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank practice. The Taylor rule shaped how policy is described and evaluated. Calvo pricing is the standard device for staggered price setting. Woodford's synthesis gave the framework its welfare-based, policy-relevant foundation. Few macroeconomic ideas have had such direct institutional influence.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many people (Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and others). The strongest individual claims are Taylor for the rule, Calvo for the pricing mechanism and Woodford for the integrated theory. This is a plausible three-way split, but it leaves out important contributors to the estimated DSGE strand.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The framework has been used for more than two decades through several policy regimes. Its performance in the 2008 crisis and the post-pandemic inflation has drawn criticism, though it remains the standard.
uncertainties: Attribution is diffuse and any three-person selection excludes close contributors.
Prior prizes to Lucas, Prescott, Kydland, Sargent and Sims already cover adjacent ground.
Recent inflation episodes and the rise of heterogeneous-agent models may weaken the case.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work rebuilt the long-run empirical record on top incomes and wealth using tax records and historical national-accounts-style methods. It put distribution back at the centre of economics and shaped both research agendas and public debate. As an economic historian I value the archival data construction and the long-run perspective. The data series are a lasting public good.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the main originators of the top-income series, with Zucman's later extensions to offshore wealth and distributional national accounts. The proposed pair reflects the original data and measurement contribution. Zucman's claim is real but more recent.
assessment.maturity: Largely mature for the income series (about two decades), and still developing for wealth and offshore estimates. The data have been widely adopted.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes over wealth estimates, capital-income imputation and the interpretation of r > g.
Policy advocacy may blur assessment of the scientific contribution.
Saez also appears in B014, so credit overlaps across candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the empirical work on trade shocks changed our understanding of labour-market polarisation and of the local costs of import competition. The work is highly influential and policy-relevant. It connects directly to the long-run question of how societies adjust to technological change and trade, which the 2025 prize also addressed.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure, across the task framework and the China-shock work. Dorn and Hanson are co-authors of the China-shock papers. Katz, Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu contributed to the task approach, so the task-model credit is shared more broadly. The China-shock trio is the cleaner attribution.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature. The key papers date from 2003 to 2016 and have been replicated and debated widely. The longer-run effects continue to be re-evaluated.
uncertainties: Debate over the size and persistence of the China-shock effects.
Possible overlap with recent technology-and-growth recognition.
The task-model credit is shared with people outside this trio.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law-and-finance programme showed systematically that legal origins and investor protection correlate with financial development. It opened a large comparative literature on institutions, corporate governance and finance. The cross-country data work was an innovation in itself.
assessment.attribution: The core papers are jointly authored by La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny, and credit is tightly shared. Shleifer has additional large contributions elsewhere. Proposing three of the four involves a judgment call about Vishny.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with more than 25 years of use and critique.
uncertainties: The legal-origins thesis has been challenged on both identification and interpretation grounds.
Excluding Vishny is difficult to justify.
Reputational controversies around some of the authors may affect the committee's view.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data gave the first credible, fine-grained maps of intergenerational mobility and of neighbourhood effects. The work combines data construction with quasi-experimental design and has changed the research agenda in public and labour economics. It is an important example of a new data infrastructure creating new knowledge.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear intellectual leader. Hendren is a principal co-author on the neighbourhood-effects and mobility work. Friedman and Katz also have strong claims through the broader collaborations, and the team-science structure complicates a narrow credit assignment.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The key papers are from about 2014 to 2022, and the long-run validation of the findings is still unfolding. This is more recent than the leading candidates above.
uncertainties: Timing: the work may be better recognised in a few years.
Team-based authorship makes the selection of names difficult.
Chetty also appears in B014, so credit overlaps across candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Grossman and Helpman developed the political-economy theory of trade protection (protection for sale) and, with their work on innovation and growth in the global economy, linked trade to endogenous technological change. The theoretical contribution is deep and has an unusually clear two-person attribution. It had a large influence on both trade and political economy.
assessment.attribution: The credit is essentially a clean pairing, which is a strength. Helpman has additional credit in firm-heterogeneity work (B021), so there is overlap with another candidate.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of use.
uncertainties: The 2025 prize for innovation-driven growth may reduce the committee's appetite for a related area.
The empirical validation of the political-economy model of protection is mixed.
Overlap with Helpman's role in B021.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference (double/debiased machine learning, causal forests and heterogeneous-effect estimation) extended empirical economics to high-dimensional settings with valid inference. The work is methodologically significant and is now widely used. Methodological advances of this kind have the best chance of recognition when they have visibly changed applied practice.
assessment.attribution: Chernozhukov is the lead on double machine learning, and Athey with Wager on causal forests and heterogeneous effects. Related contributions by others (Imbens, Belloni, Hansen and Newey) overlap. The proposed pair reflects the two main strands.
assessment.maturity: Relatively recent, mostly from 2016 onward. The adoption is rapid but the long-run assessment is not complete. It follows the Imbens-Angrist-Card recognition for causal methods.
uncertainties: It may be early for a prize in this area.
Attribution among many close contributors.
Athey also appears in B013 and Chernozhukov in B049, so credit overlaps across candidates.
